Patterns in FONSIs: Deliverable 6

Categorical-exclusion opportunities from prior clean-energy Findings of No Significant Impact

Published

June 24, 2026

Executive summary

This deliverable is technical support for categorical-exclusion (CE) development: which recurring clean-energy actions in prior Environmental Assessments that ended in a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) point to a CE opportunity? Under CEQ’s April 2026 CE guidance, those FONSIs are explicit, citable substantiation for a CE.

  • Every CE-shaped clean-energy candidate we found already maps to an existing CE. None needs a brand-new CE (0 to develop) and none exceeds an existing CE’s verified limits (0 to expand). The actionable opportunity is to adopt / harmonize CEs that already exist — 4 such opportunities.
  • The clearest case is transmission upgrades within existing right-of-way: 37 CE-shaped FONSIs across BLM, DOE, and the power-marketing administrations, for work TVA already covers under its CE #17.
  • These FONSIs lean heavily on committed mitigation (86% of transmission-upgrade findings, for example), so any CE built from them must encode the recurring mitigations as design criteria, not rely on case-by-case commitments.
  • Adopting a peer agency’s CE is well-precedented: of 2,105 existing federal CEs, 130 action-families are already shared across two or more agencies.
  • Net-new CEs most likely lie outside this candidate set — in the ~159 clean-energy FONSIs not yet categorized (the recommended next step).

First-pass caveat. This build is deterministic; specific action definitions and numeric limits are directional until the LLM-assisted verification pass runs. The structural findings above do not depend on those specifics.

Methodology

We start from the 452 clean-energy EA→FONSI projects (NEPATEC project_energy_type = "Clean", EA-source FONSIs). A FONSI concludes a full EA, so each is a documented federal determination that an action does not significantly affect the environment — the evidence base for a CE.

From those 452, 293 fall into a recognizable candidate action type and 53 are “CE-shaped” — bounded and low-impact enough to plausibly be a CE. The deliverable then runs three complementary analyses.

Branch 1 — Develop, expand, or adopt CEs

Each CE-shaped candidate’s action text is embedded (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) and matched against the 2,105 existing federal CEs (CE Explorer catalog). We parse each matched CE’s stated numeric bounds and classify the candidate as develop (no existing CE covers it), expand (our FONSIs exceed the CE’s verified limit), or adopt (a CE exists, but at an agency other than the ones doing these FONSIs).

Branch 2 — Mitigated-FONSI analysis

For each candidate we test whether its “no significant impact” findings stand on their own or depend on mitigation, using a dual signal: finding-level conditional language (“would be significant absent…”) plus enforceable, committed conditions in the record. We report the mitigated share per candidate, the resource areas where mitigation concentrates, and — preliminarily — the agency’s explicit significance-threshold (“boundary”) statements.

Branch 3 — Current-CE analysis

We characterize the existing CE body itself: embed all 2,105 CEs, compute cross-agency similarity, flag near-duplicates (cosine ≥ 0.85), cluster them into shared action-families (connected components), and parse numeric bounds across the catalog. This tells us what is already covered and how much agencies already share CEs — the precedent for adopt.

1. Develop, expand, or adopt CEs

Every CE-shaped clean-energy candidate already maps to an existing CE. None needs a net-new CE (0 to develop); none exceeds an existing CE’s verified limits (0 to expand). All 4 resolve to adopt — agencies are spending full EAs on actions a peer agency has already excluded.

Each row is the same pattern: a CE for the action exists (the Held by agency), but other agencies run the identical action through a full EA→FONSI and could adopt it. The match is an embedding-ranked candidate, so the specific CE should be confirmed against its eCFR text before action.

Worked example: transmission upgrades within existing right-of-way

The strongest-evidenced case: 37 CE-shaped FONSIs for in-corridor transmission upgrades (reconductoring, component replacement, minor rebuilds), across BLM, DOE, NNSA, and the power-marketing administrations in 12 states. The Tennessee Valley Authority already holds a CE for this class of work — TVA CE #17, “Routine modification, repair, and maintenance of, and minor upgrade of and addition to, existing transmission infrastructure…”

The table below lists sample FONSIs with a verbatim excerpt from the cited record, the document it came from (EA or FONSI), and the page — so each row is directly verifiable against the source.

2. Mitigated-FONSI analysis

A FONSI can mean two different things: the action is inherently low-impact, or it reaches “no significant impact” only because the applicant committed to mitigation. That distinction is central to CE development — a CE cannot lean on case-by-case mitigation, so if an action’s FONSIs are routinely mitigated, a defensible CE for it must bake those recurring mitigations in as design criteria.

Mitigated-FONSI share

The shares are high — 86% of transmission-upgrade and geothermal-exploration FONSIs, 75% of solar rely on committed mitigation. These are not obviously inherent-low-impact actions; the agencies reached “no significant impact” with conditions attached.

Solar 8 6 75% biological(4); cultural(2); public_health(1)
Temporary resource assessment / site investigation 2 1 50% cultural(1); transportation(1); water(1)

A high mitigated share is double-edged: it is a risk (the action is not unconditionally benign) but also an opportunity — when the same mitigations recur across the class (here, consistently water, biological, and cultural resources), they become the natural, codifiable conditions of a CE. Transmission and geothermal are the clearest: a strong, recurring mitigation profile an adopted CE could formalize.

Boundary language (preliminary)

Alongside mitigation we scan for the agency’s explicit significance-threshold statements — “would be significant if it exceeded X,” “an EIS would be required unless Y.” Those sentences are a CE’s natural numeric bounds. Detection currently surfaces candidate statements but is noisy, so verbatim thresholds are held back until the verification pass (see Caveats).

3. Current-CE analysis

To know whether an action is “develop,” “expand,” or “adopt,” we first mapped the entire existing federal CE body: 2,105 categorical exclusions across 78 agency units, embedded and compared to one another.

Numeric bounds in existing CEs

Only 86 of 2,105 CEs state a numeric limit (acres, miles, kV, MW); the rest are qualitative. So an “expand the stated limit” argument has few existing precedents to lean on — part of why nothing resolved to expand in Branch 1.

Cross-agency duplication

317 CEs are near-identical to a CE at a different agency, forming 130 action-families shared across two or more agencies. Adopting a peer agency’s CE is not unusual — it is how the existing landscape already works.

The largest shared families are administrative (procurement, personnel, routine maintenance) — which is the point: when an action is genuinely low-impact, agencies converge on the same CE. The clean-energy actions in Section 1 are simply ones where that convergence hasn’t happened yet.

Where net-new CEs would come from

Net-new CEs are empty here by construction: the candidate action types we hand-picked are all well-trodden, so all are already CE’d. But of the 452 clean-energy FONSIs, only 293 fell into those types — the remaining ~159 are other clean-energy actions we have not yet categorized. Net-new CEs most likely live there. The recommended next step is to cluster those un-categorized FONSI action descriptions to surface recurring categories nobody has hand-picked.

Caveats & next steps

  • Deterministic first pass. Action definitions and numeric limits are directional until the LLM-assisted extraction/verification pass runs; this report leads with the structural findings (adopt, not develop; mitigation-heavy), which do not depend on those specifics.
  • CE matches are a ranking aid, not verified coverage. Confirm each candidate CE against its eCFR text before acting on it.
  • Boundary-language detection is preliminary — the significance-threshold statements need the verification pass before any numeric bound is cited.
  • Recommended next steps: (1) verify the 4 adopt matches against the eCFR CE text; (2) run the verification pass to firm up size limits and boundary language; (3) cluster the ~159 un-categorized clean-energy FONSIs to search for net-new CEs.

For CATF: tell us which adopt opportunities to pursue, and whether to launch the net-new search — and we fold your direction into the next iteration.
